name: Ubiquinone (topical coenzyme Q10)
lead: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble, quinone compound found in cell membranes and involved in mitochondrial electron transport, and it also acts as an antioxidant. [13] It is included in some anti-aging creams, and the literature describes cosmetically applied CoQ10 as having been reported to reduce photoaging and wrinkle depth, while noting that its bioavailability through skin is poor. [2]

Formulation research has focused on delivery systems such as liposomes, microemulsions, nanoemulsions and lipid nanoparticles to carry the molecule into skin.[2][16] A 2024 review of 36 articles reports that topical CoQ10 products raised CoQ10 levels in the outer and deeper skin layers in ex vivo and in vivo work and, clinically, reduced wrinkle depth; the same literature includes manufacturer-affiliated work.[15][14]
Controlled human trials of topical CoQ10 in other settings, such as oral lichen planus and gum-surgery wound healing, are also published.[8][10]

paras: CoQ10 has a benzoquinone head and a ten-unit isoprenoid tail, is orange-yellow, and exists in oxidized, semiquinone and reduced (ubiquinol) states. [13] A compound first isolated in 1950 from horse intestinal lining was later identified as the same family, and in 1966 a study reported that the reduced form acts as an antioxidant in cells. [13]

sections.h: How it is thought to work on skin
paras: CoQ10 sits in cell membranes and carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and its reduced form, ubiquinol, acts as an antioxidant.[13] A 2024 review describes it as a lipid-soluble molecule supporting cellular energy production and antioxidant defence, whose levels fall with age and with skin stress, which is the rationale for replenishing it topically.[15]

Researchers at Beiersdorf reported that Q10-containing formulas raised ubiquinone on the skin surface and in deeper epidermal layers, that ubiquinol levels also rose (suggesting conversion to the active form), that Q10 raised energy metabolism in cultured human keratinocytes, and that treatment reduced free radicals and increased antioxidant capacity in stressed skin.[14] The Beiersdorf group is a skincare manufacturer, so the studies are manufacturer-affiliated.[14][15]

The molecule is fat-soluble and insoluble in water, and a 2010 paper preparing a liposomal CoQ10 for topical application states that the bioavailability of topical CoQ10 is poor and that practical formulations are desirable.[13][2] Later formulation papers describe a microemulsion for skin regeneration and wound healing, a nanoemulsion with improved skin permeability and anti-wrinkle efficiency, lipid nanoparticles, and co-loaded carriers combining CoQ10 with retinaldehyde for wrinkles.[16] Several of these are laboratory or ex vivo studies.
Oral CoQ10 is generally well tolerated according to Wikipedia, with occasional gastrointestinal upset, rashes and headache. [13] Topical-specific safety data are not described in these sources.

A quinone was isolated from beef-heart mitochondrial membranes in 1957, shown to transport electrons within mitochondria, later named ubiquinone, and its full structure was reported in 1958.[13] A 1966 study reported that the reduced form acts as an antioxidant in cells.[13] CoQ10 is now an ingredient in some cosmetics and energy drinks and a widely sold oral supplement.[13]

CoQ10 is sold over the counter as a supplement and as a cosmetic ingredient; Wikipedia notes that the FDA has not approved it to treat any medical condition and that manufacture is not regulated, so batches and brands can differ.[13] In appearance routines it is typically one antioxidant among several in a cream or eye product, alongside vitamins C and E.[16] Skin-care reviews list it among over-the-counter anti-ageing agents.[16]

Evidence in facial skin comes mainly from formulation and biochemical studies and a 2024 narrative review. The Beiersdorf biochemical study measured skin CoQ10 and antioxidant effects, and the review states that clinical work on topical CoQ10 has found reduced wrinkle depth.[14][15] Beyond those, human trials of topical CoQ10 exist in other settings: a randomized trial compared it with a topical corticosteroid in symptomatic oral lichen planus, and a triple-blinded pilot trial examined it for early wound healing after gum recession surgery.[8][10]
Animal research includes diabetic mouse wound healing with low-level light and topical CoQ10, and rodent eye studies of neuroprotection. [4][1][3]

card.summary: The mitochondrial antioxidant in many anti-aging creams; skin penetration is a recognized hurdle and direct wrinkle trials are scarce.
card.note: Topical trials found are in oral or eye conditions, not facial aging.

quick.overview:
Coenzyme Q10 is a compound the body makes in mitochondria, and it is added to anti-aging creams for antioxidant effects. One formulation paper says cosmetic CoQ10 has been reported to reduce photoaging, but that skin bioavailability is poor.

Human trials of topical CoQ10 identified here concern oral and eye conditions rather than wrinkles.
quick.mechanism: It carries electrons in the mitochondrial chain and its reduced form acts as an antioxidant. Delivery systems such as liposomes have been studied to improve skin uptake.
quick.risks: Oral CoQ10 is described as generally well tolerated. Topical-specific safety data were not found, and it is sold as a cosmetic or supplement rather than an approved anti-aging drug.

chain: Cream delivers CoQ10 into the upper skin layers
Skin CoQ10 and antioxidant capacity rise, supporting cell energy metabolism and scavenging free radicals
Wrinkle depth and signs of photoaging may soften
angle.text: People apply CoQ10 creams, serums and eye products as an antioxidant step in anti-ageing routines, aiming at finer lines and a fresher look. Manufacturer-linked studies report raised skin CoQ10 levels and reduced wrinkle depth, while independent facial-wrinkle trials are few.
